purpose: This medication is used to treat several types of cancer, including colorectal cancer, lung cancer, kidney cancer, cervical cancer, and certain brain tumors. It is often used in combination with other chemotherapy medicines. Your doctor chose this medicine as part of your overall cancer treatment plan.
how_it_works: Cancer tumors need to grow new blood vessels to get the nutrients and oxygen they need to survive and spread. This medicine works by blocking a protein called VEGF, which is like cutting off the tumor's blood supply. Without new blood vessels, the tumor has a harder time growing and spreading.
common_side_effects: High blood pressure, feeling tired or weak, headache, loss of appetite, diarrhea, nausea, runny or stuffy nose, mouth sores, and changes in how things taste. Some people also notice their wounds heal more slowly than usual.
warnings: This medicine can cause serious bleeding, including inside the body. It can also slow down or prevent wound healing, so tell your doctor about any planned surgeries. Rarely, it can cause serious problems like a hole forming in the stomach or intestines, blood clots, stroke, heart problems, or severe high blood pressure. Tell your doctor right away if you have chest pain, sudden severe headache, vision changes, or unusual bleeding. Do not use this medicine if you are pregnant, as it can harm your baby.
typical_dosing: This medicine is given through an IV (intravenous infusion) by a nurse or doctor in a clinic or hospital setting. The dose and how often you receive it depends on the type of cancer being treated, usually every 2 to 3 weeks. Your first infusion may take about 90 minutes; later infusions may be shorter if you tolerate it well.
